question: Google’s verification of Android developers: are we coming to the end of opensource software on our mobile phones?

From September 2026, all Android apps will be subject to prior registration and verification of the developer’s identity at Google, even when the app will not be distributed by the Google Play Store. Developers will have to provide an identity document, proof of address (for private individuals) or business identification documents, and make a one-off payment of USD 25.

Users will nevertheless be able to install an app from an unverified developer, by going through an ‘Advanced Flow’ process that discourages installation: — manual activation of development options; — compulsory restart of telephone; — 24-hour safety period for finalising installation; — final authentication by PIN or biometrics after that period.
This control boosts user protection against malware and fraud, but at the cost of subjugating open-source software to Google. In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider this verification policy to be in line with competition rules, given that Google is strengthening its position as gatekeeper on the mobile market?
Does this policy not risk allowing some Member States to block applications that are otherwise legal within the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2026) The Commission is aware of Google’s announcement to introduce this verification process starting from September 2026 in some jurisdictions (not including the EU based on publicly available information).

The Commission understands that, as a result of this process, Android will require that all apps are registered by verified developers in order to be installed on certified Android devices. The Commission is also aware of public campaigns such as ‘Keep Android Open’ which have emerged in reaction to Google’s announcement.

Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (‘DMA’)1 obliges gatekeepers like Alphabet to allow and technically enable the effective distribution of apps on their operating system through third party app stores or the web.

At the same time, the DMA also permits Google to introduce strictly necessary and proportionate measures to ensure that third-party software apps or app stores do not endanger the integrity of the hardware or operating system, provided that such measures are duly justified by Alphabet.

The Commission is actively engaged in a regulatory dialogue with Alphabet concerning Article 6(4) and is diligently monitoring Alphabet's compliance with the relevant legal framework to ensure that apps, including open-source apps, can be effectively distributed on Android outside Google Play.
